claim: Facultative parthenogenesis (FP) has been reported in bony fish.
source: Incidences of facultative parthenogenesis (FP) have been reported to occur in diverse vertebrate clades including bony fish (Lampert et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lampert et al., 2007.

claim: Facultative parthenogenesis (FP) has been reported in sharks.
source: Incidences of facultative parthenogenesis (FP) have been reported to occur in diverse vertebrate clades including bony fish (Lampert et al., 2007), sharks (Chapman et al., 2007; Chapman et al., 2008; Feldheim et al., 2010; Dudgeon et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to Chapman et al., 2007; Chapman et al., 2008; Feldheim et al., 2010; Dudgeon et al., 2017.

claim: Facultative parthenogenesis (FP) has been reported in snakes.
source: Incidences of facultative parthenogenesis (FP) have been reported to occur in diverse vertebrate clades including bony fish (Lampert et al., 2007), sharks (Chapman et al., 2007; Chapman et al., 2008; Feldheim et al., 2010; Dudgeon et al., 2017), snakes (Dubach et al., 1997; Groot et al., 2003; Booth and Schuett, 2011; Germano and Smith, 2010; Booth et al., 2012; Kinney et al., 2013; Booth et al., 2014; Allen et al., 2018; Card et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on snakes.

claim: Facultative parthenogenesis (FP) has been reported in lizards.
source: Incidences of facultative parthenogenesis (FP) have been reported to occur in diverse vertebrate clades including bony fish (Lampert et al., 2007), sharks (Chapman et al., 2007; Chapman et al., 2008; Feldheim et al., 2010; Dudgeon et al., 2017), snakes (Dubach et al., 1997; Groot et al., 2003; Booth and Schuett, 2011; Germano and Smith, 2010; Booth et al., 2012; Kinney et al., 2013; Booth et al., 2014; Allen et al., 2018; Card et al., 2021), lizards (Lenk et al., 2005; Watts et al., 2006; Kratochvíl et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lenk et al., 2005; Watts et al., 2006; Kratochvíl et al., 2020.

claim: Facultative parthenogenesis (FP) has been reported in crocodilians.
source: Incidences of facultative parthenogenesis (FP) have been reported to occur in diverse vertebrate clades including bony fish (Lampert et al., 2007), sharks (Chapman et al., 2007; Chapman et al., 2008; Feldheim et al., 2010; Dudgeon et al., 2017), snakes (Dubach et al., 1997; Groot et al., 2003; Booth and Schuett, 2011; Germano and Smith, 2010; Booth et al., 2012; Kinney et al., 2013; Booth et al., 2014; Allen et al., 2018; Card et al., 2021), lizards (Lenk et al., 2005; Watts et al., 2006; Kratochvíl et al., 2020), crocodilians (Booth et al., 2023)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Booth et al., 2023.

claim: Facultative parthenogenesis (FP) has been reported in birds.
source: Incidences of facultative parthenogenesis (FP) have been reported to occur in diverse vertebrate clades including bony fish (Lampert et al., 2007), sharks (Chapman et al., 2007; Chapman et al., 2008; Feldheim et al., 2010; Dudgeon et al., 2017), snakes (Dubach et al., 1997; Groot et al., 2003; Booth and Schuett, 2011; Germano and Smith, 2010; Booth et al., 2012; Kinney et al., 2013; Booth et al., 2014; Allen et al., 2018; Card et al., 2021), lizards (Lenk et al., 2005; Watts et al., 2006; Kratochvíl et al., 2020), crocodilians (Booth et al., 2023), and birds (Bartelmez and Riddle, 1924; Olsen and Marsden, 1954; Sarvella, 1973; Schut et al., 2008; Ramachandran and McDaniel, 2018; Parker et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on birds.

claim: FP was originally mistaken for long-term sperm storage in zoo environments.
source: The phenomenon was originally mistaken for long-term sperm storage occurring in zoo environments where females were housed without current or recent access to conspecific males.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Microsatellite and AFLP analyses revealed no paternal contributions in FP offspring.
source: However, more recent studies involving microsatellite (MS) and/or amplified fragment length polymorphism (AFLP) analyses revealed no paternal contributions, as all alleles detected in the offspring were only found in the maternal ancestors (Groot et al., 2003; Booth and Schuett, 2011; Shibata et al., 2017; Ryder et al., 2021; Levine et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies using MS and AFLP analyses.

claim: FP occurs in natural populations as well as in captivity.
source: Originally thought to only occur in captivity, more recent reports indicate that FP occurs in natural populations as well (Booth et al., 2012; Fields et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Booth et al., 2012 and Fields et al., 2015.

claim: Endangered species are overrepresented among reports of FP.
source: Serious concerns have been raised by conservation biologists, as species with dwindling population densities, including the endangered species Komodo dragon (Watts et al., 2006), small tooth sawfish (Fields et al., 2015), California condor (Ryder et al., 2021), and American crocodile (Booth et al., 2023) are overrepresented among reports of FP.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on endangered species showing FP.

claim: The high level of homozygosity in FP animals has been interpreted as evidence for polar body fusion following meiosis II.
source: The high level of homozygosity observed in animals produced by FP has been interpreted as evidence for polar body fusion following meiosis II, also known as automixis, leading to the restoration of diploidy in unfertilized eggs (Figure 1A; Chapman et al., 2007; Card et al., 2021; Booth et al., 2023; Booth and Schuett, 2016; Reynolds et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies and a reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Central automixis results in homozygosity concentrated near chromosome ends and heterozygosity near centromeres.
source: If automixis involves the fusion of one of the meiotic products from the first polar body (central automixis), homozygosity will be concentrated near the chromosome ends and heterozygosity will be preferentially retained near the centromeres as premeiotic recombination strongly favors homologs over sister chromatids and homologs segregate during the first meiotic division.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of meiotic processes and recombination patterns.

claim: Terminal automixis results in heterozygosity preferentially near chromosome termini.
source: In contrast, a second polar body fusion (terminal automixis) would reunite sister chromatids, for which heterozygosity is preferentially seen near the chromosome termini (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of meiotic processes and is illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Lower levels of heterozygosity in next-generation sequencing data suggest terminal automixis in snakes and crocodiles.
source: Central and terminal automixis are also distinguished by the extent of heterozygosity, with lower levels observed in next-generation sequencing data in snakes and crocodiles suggesting terminal automixis as the likely mechanism (Allen et al., 2018; Card et al., 2021; Booth et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies using next-generation sequencing data.

claim: Obligate parthenogenesis in squamate reptiles is limited to a few taxa including North American whiptail lizards of the genus Aspidoscelis.
source: While facultative parthenogenesis occurs in a wide range of vertebrate species, true obligate parthenogenesis is limited to a few taxa of squamate reptiles including the North American whiptail lizards of the genus Aspidoscelis (Avise, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Avise, 2015.

claim: Historic hybridization events in Aspidoscelis have given rise to all-female lineages capable of clonal reproduction.
source: Historic hybridization events between distinct gonochoristic species in this clade has given rise to numerous hybrid individuals with the ability to reproduce clonally as all female lineages (Vanzolini, 1993; Reeder et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vanzolini, 1993 and Reeder et al., 2002.

claim: Obligate parthenogenetic species preserve high heterozygosity from founding hybridization events.
source: In contrast to the increased homozygosity associated with FP, obligate parthenogenetic species are characterized by the long-term preservation of the high degree of heterozygosity that had its origin in the lineage-founding cross-species hybridization events.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the contrast between FP and obligate parthenogenesis.

claim: MS analysis revealed over 20 incidences of FP in A. marmoratus and A. arizonae.
source: MS analysis revealed over 20 incidences of FP in the marbled whiptail lizard, A. marmoratus and the Arizona striped whiptail, A. arizonae.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from microsatellite analysis conducted in this study.

claim: Whiptail lizards have an XX/XY sex determination system.
source: Whiptail lizards have an XX/XY sex determination system (Cole et al., 1969) and all FP offspring are consequently female.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cole et al., 1969.

claim: All FP offspring in whiptail lizards are female.
source: Whiptail lizards have an XX/XY sex determination system (Cole et al., 1969) and all FP offspring are consequently female.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the XX/XY sex determination system and the mechanism of FP.

claim: Three female A. marmoratus were housed with a male A. arizonae and a male A. gularis for close to three years.
source: In the context of studying interspecific hybridization among gonochoristic species of whiptail lizards, three female A. marmoratus (ID 122, 4238, 4239) were housed with a male A. arizonae (ID 4272) and a male A. gularis (ID 302) for close to three years.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental setup and is directly stated in the text.

claim: Seven hybrid offspring between A. marmoratus 122 and A. arizonae 4272 were produced and confirmed by MS analysis.
source: During this period, seven hybrid offspring between A. marmoratus 122 and A. arizonae 4272 were produced and confirmed by MS analysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by microsatellite analysis data from this study.

claim: Two female hatchlings (ID 8449 and 8450) resembled A. marmoratus rather than hybrids.
source: Surprisingly, two female hatchlings emerged that resembled A. marmoratus rather than the expected products of hybridization with either A. arizonae or A. gularis.
evidence: The claim is based on morphological observation.

claim: Genotyping revealed only a single allele for each of eight MS markers in offspring ID 8449 and 8450.
source: Genotyping revealed only a single allele for each of eight MS markers in the two offspring (ID 8449 and 8450, Figure 1D) and identified A. marmoratus (ID 122) as the mother (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by microsatellite genotyping data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A. marmoratus ID 122 was identified as the mother of offspring 8449 and 8450.
source: Genotyping revealed only a single allele for each of eight MS markers in the two offspring (ID 8449 and 8450, Figure 1D) and identified A. marmoratus (ID 122) as the mother (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by microsatellite analysis data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: All alleles found in offspring 8449 and 8450 were also present in the mother (ID 122).
source: Further supporting a uniparental origin of 8449 and 8450, all alleles found in the offspring were also present in the mother (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by microsatellite data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: For seven of eight markers, neither male shared the allele found in offspring 8449 and 8450.
source: For seven of the eight markers, neither male shared the allele found in the hatchling lizards, providing strong evidence that neither male fathered the offspring.
evidence: The claim is supported by microsatellite analysis data.

claim: Offspring 8449 and 8450 inherited different alleles from the mother at two markers (MS7 and MS15).
source: It is important to note that for two of the markers (MS7 and MS15), the two offspring inherited different alleles from the mother, indicating that they are not genetically identical to each other, but have randomly inherited one of the maternal alleles at each locus.
evidence: The claim is supported by microsatellite data.

claim: Two additional eggs (ID 8394 and 9070) from the same enclosure contained developing embryos with complete homozygosity at all loci.
source: Two additional eggs (ID 8394 and 9070) were recovered from the same enclosure and found to contain developing embryos. MS analysis also revealed A. marmoratus 122 as the mother and complete homozygosity at all loci.
evidence: The claim is supported by microsatellite analysis data.

claim: Animal 122 had no history of being housed with a conspecific male during its lifetime.
source: Given that all of these offspring are female, inherited only maternal alleles, and animal 122 had no history of being housed with a conspecific male during its lifetime, both interspecific hybridization and long-term sperm storage are all but ruled out and FP is strongly supported.
evidence: The claim is based on husbandry records.

claim: The A. marmoratus genome is distributed over 23 chromosomes.
source: The A. marmoratus genome is distributed over 23 chromosomes as previously demonstrated by metaphase spread analysis (Lowe and Wright, 1966).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lowe and Wright, 1966.

claim: The haploid genome size for A. marmoratus is 1.55 Gb.
source: The nuclear DNA content of A. marmoratus was close to that of Danio rerio (1.4 Gb) and we calculated a haploid genome size for A. marmoratus of 1.55 Gb (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The A. marmoratus genome assembly has a scaffold N50 of 32.22 Mb.
source: The subsequent addition of Chicago reads and scaffolding with the HiRise pipeline by Dovetail Genomics produced an assembly of 1,639,530,780 bp distributed over 3826 scaffolds (Supplementary file 1) and raised the scaffold N50 to 32.22 Mb (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by assembly statistics shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The A. marmoratus genome assembly has a BUSCO completeness score of 96%.
source: With a BUSCO completeness score of 96% the A. marmoratus genome assembly is comparable to other recently released reptilian genome assemblies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by BUSCO analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Over 98% of the A. marmoratus assembled sequences are contained within 90 scaffolds of more than 1 Mb in length.
source: Over 98% of the assembled sequences are contained within 90 scaffolds of more than 1 Mb in length, making this assembly highly contiguous.
evidence: The claim is based on assembly statistics.

claim: A. marmoratus is most closely related to the tegu Salvator merianae.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of shared BUSCO genes with several other reference genomes (Xenopus, zebrafish, medaka, platyfish, tegu, green anole, chicken, mouse, rat, dog, cow, human) confirmed that A. marmoratus is most closely related to the tegu Salvator merianae, another representative of the family Teiidae (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: All classes of repeat elements combined amount to 40.27% of the A. marmoratus assembly.
source: All classes of repeat elements combined amounted to 40.27% of the A. marmoratus assembly, only slightly below that found in other lizards S. merianae and Anolis carolinensis (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by repeat analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Unclassified repeats make up the largest class of repeat elements in the A. marmoratus genome.
source: Strikingly, unclassified repeats make up the largest class of repeat elements in the A. marmoratus genome, an observation that parallels findings in S. merianae.
evidence: The claim is supported by repeat analysis data.

claim: Only around 10% of the unclassified repeats are shared between A. marmoratus and S. merianae.
source: However, a comparison between the unclassified repeats found in A. marmoratus, S. merianae, and A. carolinensis revealed few similarities with only around 10% of the unclassified repeats shared between A. marmoratus and S. merianae, and no significant overlap between these two species and A. carolinensis (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative repeat analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The MAKER2 gene annotation pipeline yielded 25,856 protein-coding genes and 44,461 protein isoforms.
source: These transcripts were subsequently used in the MAKER2 gene annotation pipeline, yielding 25,856 protein-coding genes and 44,461 protein isoforms (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by annotation data.

claim: 76% of the putative protein-coding genes had significant hits in the UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot database.
source: To assign a putative function, we used BLASTp to query the UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot database (UniProt Consortium, 2018) and found significant hits for 76% of the putative protein-coding genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by BLAST analysis data.

claim: The A. marmoratus assembly contains 40 HOX genes and 2 EVX genes in four gene clusters.
source: Our assembly and annotation pipelines yielded 40 HOX genes and 2 EVX genes in four gene clusters (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by annotation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: For FP animals, the number of heterozygous sites in a 10 Kb sliding window approaches zero for all sites with mean coverage.
source: For FP animals, the number of heterozygous sites in a 10 Kb sliding window approaches zero for all sites with mean coverage (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Sexually produced mothers and control animals had between 30,769 and 53,416 heterozygous sites at average coverage.
source: This generated between 30,769 and 53,416 heterozygous sites for which two alleles were equally supported in the sexually produced mothers and control animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 6A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6A–E.

claim: FP animals had between 649 and 928 heterozygous sites at average coverage.
source: Far fewer heterozygous sites (between 649 and 928) were observed in the FP animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 6F–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6F–J.

claim: Heterozygous sites in FP animals are randomly distributed across the genome.
source: Plotting the heterozygous sites according to their position in the reference genome illustrates not only their sparsity in the genomes of FP animals, but also reveals their random distribution (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by visualization of heterozygous sites shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The few apparently heterozygous sites in FP animals are most likely the result of over-assembly of repetitive regions and biological/technical errors.
source: The few apparently heterozygous sites identified in FP animals are, therefore, not supporting either form of automixis but are most likely the result of over-assembly of repetitive regions (ie. collapsing paralogous loci into a single representative sequence) and a combination of biological (ie. somatic mutations) and technical errors (ie. PCR and sequencing errors).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data and knowledge of sequencing artifacts.

claim: Scaffold 45 harbors 167 genes annotated as homologous to vomeronasal 2 receptor 26 (Vmn2r26).
source: Examination of the scaffold in question (Scaffold 45) revealed 167 genes annotated as homologous to vomeronasal 2 receptor 26 (Vmn2r26; Figure 2—figure supplement 7, Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by annotation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7 and Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: The elevated level of apparent heterozygosity in Scaffold 45 is most likely due to over-assembly.
source: Given that this genomic region harbors a large cluster of highly similar genes, the most parsimonious explanation for the elevated level of apparent heterozygosity is over-assembly.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the presence of highly similar genes.

claim: The analysis strongly supports genome-wide homozygosity for FP animals.
source: In aggregate, our analysis strongly supports genome-wide homozygosity for FP animals, inconsistent with either central or terminal automixis.
evidence: The claim is based on the comprehensive analysis of heterozygosity across the genome.

claim: The results favor a post-meiotic mechanism that restores diploidy by replicating the haploid genome in the oocyte.
source: Instead, the results favor a post-meiotic mechanism that restores diploidy by replicating the haploid genome residing in the oocyte following completion of the two meiotic divisions and thereby establishing genome-wide homozygosity in the offspring.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the genome-wide homozygosity data.

claim: No cases of FP were identified among 80 A. gularis produced eggs in captivity.
source: While no cases of FP were identified among 80 A. gularis produced eggs in captivity, we identified eight incidences of FP among 832 A. arizonae records between October 2007 and July 2018.
evidence: The claim is based on microsatellite analysis of captive breeding records.

claim: Eight incidences of FP were identified among 832 A. arizonae records between October 2007 and July 2018.
source: While no cases of FP were identified among 80 A. gularis produced eggs in captivity, we identified eight incidences of FP among 832 A. arizonae records between October 2007 and July 2018.
evidence: The claim is based on microsatellite analysis of captive breeding records.

claim: 15 incidences of FP were recorded among 286 A. marmoratus records during the same period.
source: During the same period, we recorded 15 incidences of FP among 286 A. marmoratus records (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: The claim is based on microsatellite analysis of captive breeding records.

claim: In all cases, eggs undergoing FP development had been laid in enclosures where females were housed with males.
source: Notably, in all cases, eggs undergoing FP development had been laid in enclosures where females were housed with conspecific males or males of a sister species known to mate with the heterospecific females.
evidence: The claim is based on husbandry records.

claim: Isolation from mating partners was not a significant factor in triggering FP.
source: Isolation from mating partners was thus not a significant factor in triggering FP.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that FP occurred in the presence of males.

claim: A single clutch from A. arizonae female 12852 contained both sexually produced and FP offspring.
source: MS analysis of four hatchlings that originated from a single clutch laid in this enclosure identified animal 12852 as the mother of all four animals. Unexpectedly, two of her offspring were homozygous at all eight loci examined, whereas the two others were heterozygous at all loci, identifying animal 12849 as their father (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microsatellite analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both fertilized and unfertilized eggs developed alongside each other within the same clutch.
source: Therefore, both fertilized and unfertilized eggs developed alongside each other within the same clutch.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the microsatellite data showing both sexual and FP offspring in one clutch.

claim: Blood from a newly hatched FP lizard showed bimodality in erythrocyte nuclear sizes.
source: Microscopic examination of blood from a newly hatched FP lizard revealed a striking bimodality in the sizes of erythrocyte nuclei when compared to a sexually produced animals (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopic examination shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Approximately 10% of red blood cells from the FP animal harbored smaller nuclei consistent with half the amount of DNA.
source: Whereas most cells closely resembled those observed in the blood from the sexually produced animal, approximately 10% of red blood cells from the FP animal harbored smaller nuclei, consistent with half the amount of DNA (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopic examination and cell counting shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 1.27% of erythrocytes from the FP animal contained two small nuclei.
source: In addition, 1.27% contained two small nuclei, indicating that the final cytokinesis during erythrocyte differentiation had failed for some haploid progenitor cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopic examination and cell counting.

claim: DNA content analysis by flow cytometry confirmed the presence of haploid cells in FP animal blood.
source: DNA content analysis by flow cytometry confirmed the presence of haploid cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In the blood of sexually produced animals, no haploid or bi-nucleated cells were observed.
source: In the blood of sexually produced animals, no haploid or bi-nucleated cells were observed.
evidence: The claim is based on microscopic examination of control animals.

claim: Embryonic development of FP animals may be initiated with consecutive divisions of a haploid, unfertilized oocyte.
source: These observations raise the possibility that the embryonic development of FP animals is initiated with consecutive divisions of a haploid, unfertilized oocyte.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observation of haploid cells in FP animals.

claim: Diploid cells in FP animals most likely arise via failed cytokinesis at a later stage in development.
source: At a later stage in development, diploid cells most likely arise via failed cytokinesis.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the presence of both haploid and diploid cells.

claim: Both haploid and diploid cells coexist in FP embryos, developing in a mixoploid state.
source: From that point forward, both haploid and diploid cells coexist, and the embryo develops in a mixoploid state.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of both haploid and diploid cells in FP animals.

claim: Mixoploidy was also observed in another FP A. marmoratus and in A. arizonae.
source: Indicative of a more widespread phenomenon, mixoploidy was also observed in another FP A. marmoratus and in A. arizonae (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopic examination shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Genome-wide loss of heterozygosity exposes functionally compromised alleles.
source: Genome-wide loss of heterozygosity exposes functionally compromised alleles that were previously covered by intact alleles on the homologous chromosomes.
evidence: The claim is based on established genetic knowledge.

claim: Of the 23 incidences of FP examined, only 14 hatched.
source: Indeed, of the 23 incidences of FP examined here, only 14 hatched, while the remaining lizards died in ovum (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: The claim is based on husbandry records.

claim: Notable developmental defects in FP animals included craniofacial abnormalities, missing limbs, and failed abdominal closure.
source: Notable developmental defects included craniofacial abnormalities such as misaligned jaws, agenesis of eyes, missing limbs, and failed abdominal closure (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by photographic documentation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Only six out of 16 FP animals (37.5%) hatched with no discernable developmental defects.
source: Only six out of 16 FP animals (37.5%) hatched with no discernable developmental defects (Figure 4—figure supplement 2 A-B).
evidence: The claim is based on phenotypic assessment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Over 98% of sexually produced hatchlings (n=687) showed no abnormalities.
source: This is in stark contrast to sexually produced animals, where over 98% of hatchlings (n=687) showed no abnormalities.
evidence: The claim is based on phenotypic assessment of control animals.

claim: FP A. marmoratus 8450 produced two eggs while housed in isolation, but these failed to hatch.
source: While we have not recorded instances of FP animals producing offspring via FP, as described for the whitespotted bamboo shark (Straube et al., 2016), FP A. marmoratus 8450 did produce two eggs while housed in isolation, but these failed to hatch.
evidence: The claim is based on husbandry records.

claim: Analysis of ovaries and germinal vesicles of FP animals revealed no differences compared to fertile sexually reproducing animals.
source: Analysis of the ovaries of FP animal 8450 as well as germinal vesicles of its FP sister 8449 revealed no differences in structure and anatomy compared to fertile sexually reproducing animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopic examination shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: RAD-seq data was examined for wild animals across 15 gonochoristic species.
source: As FP has been associated with captivity in most species where it has been reported, we examined restriction site-associated DNA sequencing (RAD-seq) data for wild animals across 15 gonochoristic species (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim describes the analysis performed and is shown in Figure 5.

claim: 321 individuals with an average sequencing coverage of at least 20 were analyzed.
source: Because RAD-seq is a form of reduced-representation sequencing (Rivera-Colón and Catchen, 2022), we limited further analysis to the 321 individuals that had an average sequencing coverage of at least 20.
evidence: The claim describes the filtering criteria for the analysis.

claim: Five animals (one A. angusticeps and four A. deppii) had very low levels of heterozygosity (<0.05%).
source: Computational data analysis revealed five animals (one A. angusticeps and four A. deppii) that had very low levels of heterozygosity at positions of average coverage (<0.05% heterozygous positions).
evidence: The claim is based on RAD-seq data analysis.

claim: The average level of heterozygosity across the RAD-seq dataset was 0.261%.
source: In contrast, the average level of heterozygosity was 0.261% across the dataset, with the highest heterozygosity value at 0.578%.
evidence: The claim is based on RAD-seq data analysis.

claim: A. deppii (ID LDOR30) showed the most striking level of homozygosity with all sites but one being homozygous.
source: Of the five low heterozygosity animals, A. deppii (ID LDOR30) showed the most striking level of homozygosity affecting all sites but one (Rosner's Test for Outliers within A. deppii individuals, log-transformation, R=5.127, λ=3.928, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by RAD-seq data analysis and statistical testing.

claim: FP occurring in A. marmoratus and A. arizonae results in genome-wide homozygosity.
source: Here, we show that FP occurring in the gonochoristic Aspidoscelis species A. marmoratus and A. arizonae results in genome-wide homozygosity, an observation inconsistent with polar body fusion as the underlying mechanism of restoration.
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data.

claim: A post-meiotic mechanism gives rise to homozygous animals from haploid, unfertilized oocytes.
source: Instead, a high-quality reference genome for A. marmoratus and analysis of whole-genome sequencing from multiple FP and control animals reveals that a post-meiotic mechanism gives rise to homozygous animals from haploid, unfertilized oocytes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from genome-wide homozygosity data.

claim: Females housed with conspecific and heterospecific males produced unfertilized eggs that underwent spontaneous development.
source: Contrary to the widely held belief that females need to be isolated from males to undergo FP, females housed with conspecific and heterospecific males produced unfertilized eggs that underwent spontaneous development.
evidence: The claim is based on husbandry records and microsatellite analysis.

claim: Offspring arising from both fertilized eggs and parthenogenetic development were observed in a single clutch.
source: In addition, offspring arising from both fertilized eggs and parthenogenetic development were observed to arise from a single clutch.
evidence: The claim is supported by microsatellite analysis of a single clutch.

claim: The mechanism for facultative parthenogenesis removes all heterozygosity in a single generation.
source: Strikingly, our data support a mechanism for facultative parthenogenesis that removes all heterozygosity in a single generation.
evidence: The claim is based on genome-wide homozygosity data.

claim: Complete homozygosity exposes the genetic load and explains the high rate of congenital malformations and embryonic mortality associated with FP.
source: Complete homozygosity exposes the genetic load and explains the high rate of congenital malformations and embryonic mortality associated with FP in many species.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from genetic principles and observed developmental defects.

claim: For animals that develop normally, FP could potentially exert strong purifying selection as all lethal recessive alleles are purged in a single generation.
source: Conversely, for animals that develop normally, FP could potentially exert strong purifying selection as all lethal recessive alleles are purged in a single generation.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the mechanism of FP.

claim: The start of embryonic development is tightly coupled to fertilization in many vertebrates.
source: The start of embryonic development is tightly coupled to fertilization in many vertebrates as the sperm entering the oocyte triggers a signaling cascade that is essential for the completion of female meiosis and initiation of cell division following karyogamy (Sagata, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sagata, 1996 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Piercing frog oocytes with a needle can trigger the signal to complete meiosis and initiate replication and division in the haploid oocyte.
source: This process has been mimicked in the laboratory by piercing frog oocytes with a needle to trigger the signal to complete meiosis and initiate replication and division in the haploid oocyte (Le Peuch et al., 1985; Wolf, 1974).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Le Peuch et al., 1985 and Wolf, 1974.

claim: In zebrafish, homozygous embryos are routinely generated by fertilization of oocytes with UV-irradiated sperm.
source: In zebrafish, homozygous embryos are routinely generated by fertilization of oocytes with UV-irradiated sperm, a treatment that destroys the paternal DNA (Streisinger et al., 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Streisinger et al., 1981.

claim: Heat shock treatment of zebrafish oocytes prevents cytokinesis resulting in a pseudodiploid oocyte.
source: If the haploid oocyte is then subjected to heat shock treatment, cytokinesis is prevented resulting in a pseudodiploid oocyte that undergoes a second round of DNA replication followed by mitosis. Thus an entirely homozygous diploid embryo starts to develop (Kroeger et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kroeger et al., 2014.

claim: One or multiple rounds of DNA replication and mitosis take place in some haploid oocytes of whiptail lizards prior to a skipped mitosis yielding a homozygous diploid cell.
source: In contrast to human intervention forcing two consecutive rounds of DNA replication to occur without intervening mitosis at the start of embryonic development, our data indicate that one or multiple rounds of DNA replication and mitosis take place in some haploid oocytes of whiptail lizards prior to a skipped mitosis yielding a homozygous diploid cell followed by mixoploid development.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation of mixoploidy in FP animals.

claim: Unfertilized turkey eggs can yield embryos that contain 40% of haploid cells at blastoderm followed by a reduction to 1.3% within the blood of hatched birds.
source: Initiation of development in a haploid state may be conserved in avian species as unfertilized turkey eggs can yield embryos that contain 40% of haploid cells at blastoderm followed by a reduction to 1.3% within the blood of hatched birds (Cassar et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cassar et al., 1998.

claim: The presence of haploid cells may contribute to abnormal development of specific tissues.
source: Depending on the tissue and ploidy distribution, the presence of haploid cells may contribute to abnormal development of specific tissues reported here and elsewhere (Ito et al., 1991; Tanaka et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is speculative, supported by citations to Ito et al., 1991 and Tanaka et al., 2004.

claim: Successful embryonic development from haploid cells that restore the diploid state by duplication has been observed in a stick insect species.
source: Successful embryonic development from haploid cells that restore the diploid state by duplication has also been observed in a stick insect species (Pijnacker, 1969).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pijnacker, 1969.

claim: FP leads to a precipitous reduction in genetic diversity as only one set of alleles is inherited in the next generation.
source: At the population level, FP leads to a precipitous reduction in genetic diversity as only one set of alleles is inherited in the next generation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the mechanism of FP.

claim: FP can be considered the most extreme example of inbreeding.
source: While FP can be considered the most extreme example of inbreeding, it is also the most powerful example of genetic purging as it eliminates most deleterious alleles in a single generation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the mechanism of FP and genetic principles.

claim: FP in whiptail lizards and other species could be considered a reproductive strategy, akin to mixed-mating systems in plants.
source: FP in whiptail lizards and other species could, therefore, be considered a reproductive strategy, akin to mixed-mating systems in plants (Goodwillie et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is speculative, drawing an analogy to plant mating systems with citation to Goodwillie et al., 2005.

claim: The ability to produce offspring via two different strategies provides a level of reproductive assurance in plants.
source: The ability to produce offspring via two different strategies provides a level of reproductive assurance in plants (Busch and Delph, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Busch and Delph, 2012.

claim: Female whiptails have produced offspring via both sexual reproduction and FP on separate occasions or simultaneously within a single clutch.
source: Indeed, we see parallels to this in our own data in which female whiptails have produced offspring via both sexual reproduction and FP on separate occasions or simultaneously within a single clutch.
evidence: The claim is based on microsatellite analysis data from this study.

claim: Recent work identified key cell cycle genes inducing FP in two species of Drosophila.
source: Recent work identifying key cell cycle genes inducing FP in two species of Drosophila (Sperling et al., 2023) and selection resulting in higher incidences of parthenogenesis in birds (Parker et al., 2010; Olsen, 1975; Olsen et al., 1968) suggest a genetic basis for the initiation of FP.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sperling et al., 2023.

claim: Selection has resulted in higher incidences of parthenogenesis in birds.
source: Recent work identifying key cell cycle genes inducing FP in two species of Drosophila (Sperling et al., 2023) and selection resulting in higher incidences of parthenogenesis in birds (Parker et al., 2010; Olsen, 1975; Olsen et al., 1968) suggest a genetic basis for the initiation of FP.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Parker et al., 2010; Olsen, 1975; Olsen et al., 1968.

claim: This study adds two species of whiptail lizards to the list of vertebrates capable of FP.
source: Our study adds two species of whiptail lizards to a growing list of vertebrates capable of FP and establishes that it occurs alongside sexual reproduction in the presence of males.
evidence: The claim is based on the findings of this study.

claim: FP occurs alongside sexual reproduction in the presence of males in whiptail lizards.
source: Our study adds two species of whiptail lizards to a growing list of vertebrates capable of FP and establishes that it occurs alongside sexual reproduction in the presence of males.
evidence: The claim is based on husbandry records and microsatellite analysis from this study.

claim: Post-meiotic genome duplication is the underlying mechanism of FP in whiptail lizards.
source: Using whole-genome sequencing, we demonstrate that post-meiotic genome duplication is the underlying mechanism.
evidence: The claim is based on whole-genome sequencing data showing genome-wide homozygosity.

claim: Low rates of successful FP could contribute significantly to genome purification.
source: One must now consider the possibility that FP is an adaptive trait and that low rates of successful FP could contribute significantly to genome purification.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the mechanism of FP.

claim: Sexually mature FP offspring will have a low genetic load and only pass on neutral or mildly deleterious alleles to the next generation.
source: Sexually mature FP offspring will have a low genetic load and only pass on neutral or mildly deleterious alleles to the next generation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the purifying selection mechanism of FP.

claim: A role for FP as an adaptive trait hinges on the ability of parthenogens to reproduce themselves either through further FP or sexually.
source: However, a role for FP as an adaptive trait hinges on further studies demonstrating the ability of parthenogens to reproduce themselves either through further FP or sexually.
evidence: The claim is speculative, identifying a condition for FP to be adaptive.

claim: FP may reduce the frequency of deleterious alleles within a population.
source: If successive reproduction occurs, FP may reduce the frequency of deleterious alleles within a population, as well as provide reproductive assurance when males are scarce.
evidence: The claim is speculative, conditional on successive reproduction of FP offspring.
